example.paragraph: Let $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} - xy$$ . Find $$\Delta z$$ . Then use your result to find the change in $$z$$ if $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ changes from $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0.98,1.03} \right)$$ .

note.title: Total Differential
note.heading: Total Differential
note.paragraph: Let $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ define a differentiable function of $$x$$ and $$y$$ .

list.item: The differentials of the independent variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ are $$dx = \Delta x$$ and $$dy = \Delta y$$ .
The differential of the dependent variable $$z$$ is (17) $$dz = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}dy$$

section.paragraph: Thus, analogous to the one-variable case, the total differential of $$z$$ is a linear function of $$dx$$ and $$dy$$ . Furthermore, it provides us with an approximation of the exact change in $$z$$ ,
corresponding to a net change $$\Delta x$$ in $$x$$ from $$x$$ to $$x + \Delta x$$ and a net change $$\Delta y$$ in $$y$$ from $$y$$ to $$y + \Delta y$$ ; that is,
$$\Delta z \approx dz = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}\left( {x,y} \right)dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}\left( {x,y} \right)dy$$
provided that $$\Delta x = dx$$ and $$\Delta y = dy$$ are sufficiently small.

example.heading: Example 2

list.item: Find the approximate change in $$z$$ when $$x$$ changes from $$x = 1$$ to $$x = 1.01$$ and $$y$$ changes from $$y = 2$$ to $$y = 1.98$$ .
Find the actual change in $$z$$ when $$x$$ changes from $$x = 1$$ to $$x = 1.01$$ and $$y$$ changes from $$y = 2$$ to $$y = 1.98$$ . Compare the result with that obtained in part (b).

example.heading: Solution

list.item: Let $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2}y + y^{3}$$ . Then the required differential is $$dz = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}dy = 4xydx + {({2x^{2} + 3y^{2}})}dy$$

Here $$x = 1$$ , $$y = 2$$ , and $$dx = 1.01 - 1 = 0.01$$ and $$dy = 1.98 - 2 = - 0.02$$ . Therefore, $$\Delta z \approx dz = 4(1)(2)(0.01) + \left\lbrack {2(1) + 3(4)} \right\rbrack\left( {- 0.02} \right) = - 0.20$$

The actual change in $$z$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{ll} {\Delta z} & {= f\left( {1.01,1.98} \right) - f\left( {1,2} \right)} \\ \phantom{\Delta z} & {= \left\lbrack {2(1.01)^{2}(1.98) + (1.98)^{3}} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {2(1)^{2}(2) + (2)^{3}} \right\rbrack} \\ \phantom{\Delta z} & {= 11.801988 - 12} \\ \phantom{\Delta z} & {\approx - 0.1980} \end{array}$$

example.paragraph: We see that $$\Delta z \approx dz$$ , as expected.

note.source_type: Applied Example 3. Approximating Changes in Revenue
note.title: Applied Example 3. Approximating Changes in Revenue
note.heading: Applied Example 3. Approximating Changes in Revenue
note.paragraph: The weekly total revenue of Acrosonic Company resulting from the production and sales of $$x$$ fully assembled bookshelf loudspeaker systems and $$y$$ kit versions of the same loudspeaker system is

dollars. Determine the approximate change in Acrosonic’s weekly total revenue when the level of production is increased from $$200$$ assembled units and $$60$$ kits per week to $$206$$ assembled units and $$64$$ kits per week.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: The approximate change in the weekly total revenue is given by the total differential $$R$$ at $$x = 200$$ and $$y = 60$$ , $$dx = 206 - 200 = 6$$ and $$dy = 64 - 60 = 4$$ , that is, by

$$\begin{array}{l} {dR = \frac{\partial R}{\partial x}dx + \left. \frac{\partial R}{\partial y}dy \right|_{dx = 6,dy = 4}^{x = 200,y = 60}} \\ {{\phantom{dR} = {\left( {- \frac{1}{2}x - \frac{1}{4}y + 300} \right)|}_{({200,60})}} \cdot (6)} \\ {\phantom{dR} = + \left( {- \frac{3}{4}y - \frac{1}{4}x + 240} \right)\left. \middle| {}_{({200,60})} \right. \cdot (4)} \\ {\phantom{dR} = \left( {- 100 - 15 + 300} \right)6 + \left( {- 45 - 50 + 240} \right)4} \\ {\phantom{dR} = 1690} \end{array}$$

note.title: Applied Example 4. Cobb–Douglas Production Function
note.heading: Applied Example 4. Cobb–Douglas Production Function
note.paragraph: The production for a certain country in the early years following World War II is described by the function
$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 30x^{2 \slash 3}y^{1 \slash 3}$$

units, when $$x$$ units of labor and $$y$$ units of capital were utilized. Find the approximate change in output if the amount expended on labor had been decreased from $$125$$ units to $$123$$ units and the amount expended on capital had been increased from $$27$$ to $$29$$ units. Is your result as expected given the result of Example 4c, Section 8.2?
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: The approximate change in output is given by the total differential of $$f$$ at $$x = 125$$ , $$y = 27$$ , $$dx = 123 - 125 = - 2$$ , and $$dy = 29 - 27 = 2$$ , that is, by

$$\begin{array}{l} {df = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}dx + \left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}dy \right|_{dx = - 2,dy = 2}^{x = 125,y = 27}} \\ \left. \left. \phantom{df} = 20x^{- {1 \slash 3}}y^{1 \slash 3} \right|_{({125,27})} \cdot \left( {- 2} \right) + 10x^{2 \slash 3}y^{{- 2} \slash 3} \middle| {}_{({125,27})} \cdot (2) \right. \\ {\phantom{df} = 20\left( \frac{27}{125} \right)^{1 \slash 3}\left( {- 2} \right) + 10\left( \frac{125}{27} \right)^{2 \slash 3}(2)} \\ {\phantom{df} = - 20\left( \frac{3}{5} \right)(2) + 10\left( \frac{25}{9} \right)(2) = \frac{284}{9}} \end{array}$$

or $$31\frac{5}{9}$$ units. This result is fully compatible with the result of Example 4c, Section 8.2, in which the recommendation was to encourage increased spending on capital rather than on labor.

section.paragraph: If $$f$$ is a function of the three variables $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ , then the total differential of $$w = f\left( {x,y,z} \right)$$ is defined to be
$$dw = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}dy + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}dz$$

where $$dx = \Delta x$$ , $$dy = \Delta y$$ , and $$dz = \Delta z$$ are the actual changes in the independent variables $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ as $$x$$ changes from $$x = a$$ to $$x = a + \Delta x$$ , $$y$$ changes from $$y = b$$ to $$y = b + \Delta y$$ , and $$z$$ changes from $$z = c$$ to $$z = c + \Delta z$$ , respectively.

note.title: Applied Example 5. Error Analysis
note.heading: Applied Example 5. Error Analysis
note.paragraph: Find the maximum percentage error in calculating the volume of a rectangular box if an error of at most $$1\%$$ is made in measuring the length, width, and height of the box.
note.heading: Solution
note.paragraph: Let $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ denote the length, width, and height, respectively, of the rectangular box. Then the volume of the box is given by $$V = f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xyz$$ cubic units. Now suppose that the true dimensions of the rectangular box are $$a$$ , $$b$$ , and $$c$$ units, respectively. Since the error committed in measuring the length, width, and height of the box is at most $$1\%$$ , we have

$$\begin{matrix} {\left| {\Delta x} \right| = {\left| {x - a} \right| \leq 0.01a}} \\ {\left| {\Delta y} \right| = {\left| {y - b} \right| \leq 0.01b}} \\ {\left| {\Delta z} \right| = {\left| {z - c} \right| \leq 0.01c}} \end{matrix}$$
Therefore, the maximum error in calculating the volume of the box is

$$\begin{array}{l} {\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx {|{dV}| = \left| {\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}dy + \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}dz} \middle| \right|_{x = a,y = b,z = c}}} \\ \left. \phantom{\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx \left| {dV} \right|} = \middle| yzdx + xzdy + xydz \middle| \right|_{x = a,y = b,z = c} \\ {\phantom{\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx \left| {dV} \right|}{= \left| {bcdx + acdy + abdz} \right|}} \\ {\phantom{\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx \left| {dV} \right|}{\leq bc\left| {dx} \right| + ac\left| {dy} \right| + ab\left| {dz} \right|}} \\ {\phantom{\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx \left| {dV} \right|}{\leq bc\left( {0.01a} \right) + ac\left( {0.01b} \right) + ab\left( {0.01c} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\left| {\Delta V} \right| \approx \left| {dV} \right|}{= (0.03)abc}} \end{array}$$
Since the actual volume of the box is $$abc$$ cubic units, we see that the maximum percentage error in calculating its volume is
$$\frac{\left| {\Delta V} \right|}{\left. V \right|_{({a,b,c})}} \approx \frac{(0.03)abc}{abc} = 0.03$$
that is, approximately $$3\%$$ .
